documents.abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to the primary driver of labor efficiency: minimizing the time that stations sit unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies of the push approach for a single pod, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system while increasing the standard time allotted for tasks can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons, the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

This article examines the didactic possibilities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the organization of mother tongue lessons, their role in the educational process, and their influence on the development of students' knowledge. It analyzes the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence tools for taking individual learning needs into account, differentiating language-related tasks, developing written and oral communication skills, and assessing learning. It also addresses pedagogical appropriateness, the reliability of information, and the need to maintain teacher oversight when introducing these technologies into mother tongue education. The article substantiates that the effective use of artificial intelligence can increase students' interest in language learning and help accommodate individual differences in the learning process.

Smart city policies often equate investment in digital infrastructure with sustainable urban change, thus assuming that infrastructure is simply a technical layer devoid of institutional and societal context. This study uses qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA Pro version 2024 and focuses on the “Digital Infrastructure Ecosystem” as it appears in strategic plans of Konya city (Turkiye) and Bucharest Sector 5 (Romania). The coding was performed by two independent researchers who achieved a Cohen’s Kappa of .89. The analysis reveals striking differences between the two cities in the three categories of Connectivity and Hardware, Data Security and Management, and System Integration, as Konya employs a hardware-centric development based on fiber-optic backbone, radio connections, and server infrastructure, while Bucharest seeks to migrate from installation of cables to the provision of services (public Wi-Fi, super-app). The results are assessed through the Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Vial’s digital transformation theory (2019), platform ecosystem approach, and dynamic capabilities theory, thus concluding that infrastructural investment itself is of no transformational value without institutional learning capacity and multi-actor governance mechanisms. By highlighting the conflict between “global compliance” and “local context” in the development of smart cities, the study provides a comparative and interdisciplinary contribution.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

documents.abstract: Digital self-management is increasingly used to support people with chronic non-communicable diseases between visits, but its public health value depends on integration into routine care. This SANRA-informed critical narrative mini review synthesized 28 sources identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, backward citation tracking and targeted supplementary searches. It examines digital self-management as service redesign across three delivery models: patient centered digital support, remote patient monitoring, and integrated primary care or community coordination. It also analyzes three implementation tensions: empowerment versus digital exclusion, data visibility versus clinical accountability, and engagement versus uncertain long term outcomes and workload. Evidence suggests benefits for engagement, behavioral support and selected intermediate indicators, but these benefits remain uneven. Public health implementation should therefore prioritize accountable workflows, interoperable procurement, equity oriented support, safe use of large language model based agents, and evaluation of outcomes, safety, equity, cost and workforce burden. Digital self-management should be judged by whether it supports routine, inclusive and sustainable chronic disease care.

Digital technologies are becoming increasingly embedded in undergraduate dental curricula, with the potential to support learning and skills development. This scoping review mapped recent evidence on the implementation and educational applications of contemporary digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify studies published between 2021 and 2025. The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines and included studies investigating digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A total of 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. The identified technologies included virtual reality and simulation-based learning systems, digital and 3D-printed educational models, digital assessment and feedback systems, web-based learning platforms, artificial intelligence applications, CAD/CAM technologies, and digital clinical devices. Across the included studies, the reported educational outcomes most commonly concerned practical performance, knowledge acquisition, student engagement, self-assessment, and satisfaction, with many studies focusing on short-term preclinical or learner-reported outcomes. Virtual simulation and digital assessment systems were the most extensively investigated technologies. The available evidence suggests that digital technologies may support undergraduate dental education when used as adjuncts to conventional teaching methods. However, the effectiveness of specific blended-learning models requires direct comparative evaluation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal and methodologically rigorous studies examining long-term knowledge retention, clinical competence, educational quality, and the transfer of acquired skills to professional practice.

Organic agriculture is growing rapidly in India, yet organic supply chains remain structurally fragmented, particularly in smallholder-dominated regions such as South Tamil Nadu. Digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising solutions to persistent challenges, including inadequate cold-chain infrastructure, limited traceability, intermediary-dependent marketing and certification workflow inefficiencies. This systematic review draws on evidence from 30 peer-reviewed and institutional publications. These sources were identified through a PRISMA-compliant search of Scopus, Elsevier, Taylor & Francis, Web of Science, IEEE, MDPI, Wiley, FAO, and government databases. The findings indicate that AI-enabled precision farming, machine learning-based demand forecasting, Internet of Things-enabled cold-chain monitoring, and blockchain-supported traceability improve production efficiency, market access and organic supply chain transparency. However, widespread adoption is constrained by inadequate rural connectivity, limited digital literacy, incompatibility between digital platforms and Participatory Guarantee System certification workflows, and weak first-mile infrastructure. This review proposes the Digital Transformation and AI Readiness Framework for Organic Supply Chains (DARF-OSC). DARF-OSC is a five-stage conceptual model that integrates Diffusion of Innovations theory with the Resource-Based View. Also, this review identifies five key research gaps and tiered policy recommendations for South Tamil Nadu.
topics: Digitalization and Economic Development in Agriculture

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the intersection of digital technology and cultural heritage education, focusing on the fundamental tension between technological innovation and authentic cultural engagement. Through analysis of virtual reality applications, digital storytelling, and multimedia platforms in educational contexts, this chapter explores how digital tools simultaneously expand access to cultural resources while potentially distancing students from embodied cultural experiences. The accessibility-authenticity paradox emerges as a central challenge, alongside concerns about superficial engagement and the speed of digital information consumption. This chapter proposes pedagogical frameworks for conscious technology integration, emphasizing hybrid approaches that strategically combine digital and physical cultural encounters. Recommendations address educator preparation, institutional policies, and the development of critical digital cultural literacy among students. The chapter concludes by examining emerging technologies including artificial intelligence and metaverse environments, identifying research gaps, and advocating for theoretical frameworks that balance innovation with cultural integrity in heritage education.

Food microbiology is moving from episodic, laboratory-centered testing toward connected systems that can detect, interpret, and anticipate microbial hazards across food production and distribution. This transition is being driven by the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biosensors, computer vision, spectroscopy, predictive microbiology, Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructure, and digital-twin concepts. The value of these technologies lies not in replacing reference microbiological methods, but in shortening the interval between sampling, evidence generation, risk interpretation, and corrective action. AI can extract patterns from images, spectral fingerprints, sensor signals, molecular data, and environmental measurements; biosensors can convert biological recognition into rapidly measurable signals; and connected monitoring architectures can place these outputs within dynamic process and supply-chain contexts. Recent studies demonstrate progress in deep-learning-based microbial identification, machine-learning-assisted biosensing, non-destructive hyperspectral and volatile sensing, smartphone-enabled field analysis, and predictive models that integrate temperature, pH, water activity, and other determinants of microbial behavior. However, translation from proof-of-concept studies to routine food control remains constrained by matrix effects, limited external validation, data drift, small or unrepresentative datasets, inconsistent reporting, device interoperability, cybersecurity, and uncertain regulatory pathways. This chapter examines the principal components of digital food microbiology, emphasizes their integration into practical food-safety workflows, and proposes a validation-oriented perspective for responsible deployment. The emerging paradigm is therefore best understood as augmented microbiology: conventional culture and molecular reference methods remain essential, while digital tools add speed, continuity, predictive capacity, and decision support.

Background. In the context of healthcare digital transformation, telemedicine (TM) and artificial intelligence (AI) are being integrated into clinical practice; however, the pace of their implementation outpaces the analysis of their impact on workflows, workload, and physicians’ psychological acceptance. Studying systemic barriers and the human factor is essential for the successful scaling of digital tools in primary care. Objective: to assess real-world experience, identify key barriers, and determine the relationship between physicians’ expectations and practical challenges of implementing TM and AI in the activities of outpatient medical professionals. Materials and methods. A cross-sectional study was conducted using an anonymous online survey of 897 medical professionals from outpatient clinics in the Moscow region. The questionnaire covered socio-demographic and professional characteristics, frequency and formats of TM, AI and EHR use, as well as perceived barriers and risks. Statistical analysis employed descriptive statistics and Pearson’s χ² test (p < 0.05). Results. Daily TM consultations are conducted by 49.7% of physicians, predominantly in audio format (46.5%). Despite recognizing TM effectiveness for chronic patient follow-up (63.3%), 30.6% report increased workload, and 38.3% consider no more than two consultations per day optimal. The main TM barriers are technical failures (29.3%) and low patient digital literacy (16.2%). Regarding AI, a gap was revealed: readiness for use is 55%, while 60.5% have no practical experience; 50.1% fear degradation of their diagnostic skills. Major systemic issues include insufficient interoperability (43.6%) and lack of training (22.8%). Statistical analysis confirmed significant associations between AI use and expectations (p < 0.05), and between training needs and AI readiness (χ² = 23.979; p < 0.001). Conclusion. A persistent gap was identified between positive perceptions of digital technologies’ potential and the real challenges of their integration. The barriers – technical, organizational, and psychological – are systemic and require comprehensive solutions: specialized training, minimization of technical failures, ensuring information systems interoperability, and revision of workload standards considering the time spent on TM consultations.

documents.abstract: Purpose This scoping review maps and synthesises fragmented research on disability inclusion from a workplace culture perspective and develops a definition of a disability inclusive workplace culture. Design/methodology/approach Following Arksey and O'Malley's scoping review framework, 32 empirical studies across organisational settings were systematically reviewed. The studies were charted according to their characteristics and analysed thematically. The analysis was then synthesised into a definition capturing how disability inclusive workplace cultures are constituted. Findings The review finds that disability inclusive workplace cultures comprise shared patterns of organisational structures, social practices and psychological experiences that enable employees with disabilities to access and engage meaningfully in the cultural life of the organisation. Cultural inclusion develops through the complex interaction of these dimensions, with leadership and job design acting as central mechanisms. Such cultures are characterised by diversity practices and inclusive leadership, by supportive peer relations and inclusive norms and by employees' experiences of self-confidence, belonging and fairness. In this way, a disability inclusive workplace culture represents a structural framework, a social practice and a subjective experience. Originality/value This review is the first to provide an empirically grounded definition of a disability inclusive workplace culture. The review contributes to the field of disability studies in organisations by conceptualising inclusion as a cultural phenomenon and by bringing together fragmented insights that have not previously been integrated.

This paper addresses the problem that, during the distillation of large language models, student models may remain at the level of imitating teacher models' answers and struggle to develop stable knowledge-invocation capabilities. It proposes a conceptual architecture for response-structure distillation and teacher–student blind-evaluation post-training, with the aim of developing transferable capabilities. This paper argues that, when two models have similar knowledge bases, differences in response quality may lie more in how knowledge is invoked, organized, and applied than in the amount of knowledge the models possess. Accordingly, this study proposes a distillation-first, training-second sequence in which the response structure is treated as an independent learning target: the student model learns the teacher model's response structures across different contexts, and then invokes its own existing knowledge to fill in those structures. Subsequently, the student model's responses are jointly evaluated through five sources of evaluation—a structure-evaluation model, a scoring model, domain experts, non-experts, and anonymous comparisons between the teacher and student models. The evaluation results and disagreements are fed back to the student model, and through repeated revision and subsequent training, the architecture attempts to gradually consolidate effective ways of invoking knowledge into stable, invocable paths within the student model. This paper further proposes mechanisms such as feeding structure-related feedback back into the revision process, limiting the number of iteration rounds, and generating training signals, so as to form a post-training closed loop of continuous correction. The proposed architecture aims to explore a possible path from imitating the teacher model's way of answering to developing the student model's own answering capabilities; its effectiveness and its ability to transfer to unseen contexts remain to be verified through subsequent experiments.

The digitization of education has concentrated vast volumes of sensitive learner data within centralized platforms that are priority targets for cyber attackers. It is argued that the dominant centralized model of educational artificial intelligence is structurally misaligned with modern privacy and resilience needs, and an alternative grounded in Distributed Artificial Intelligence is proposed. A layered architecture is presented that couples Federated Learning with Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents to deliver privacy-preserving analytics and autonomous cyber resilience without centralizing raw data. Learner records remain on institutional premises; model updates are protected by differential privacy and secure aggregation; and collaborative threat detection and self-healing are performed by distributed BDIx agents. BDIx-FL reached 99.17% accuracy, 98.93% macro-F1 and 99.76% macro AUC in simulation. Controversies are examined, deployment recommendations are offered and open directions are identified for educational ecosystems that are trustworthy by design.

Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent in healthcare. Unlike previous technologies, AI has the capability to perform tasks previously considered uniquely human including synthesizing historical information and data to establish a clinical diagnosis and constructing a treatment plan. AI promises to improve diagnostic accuracy, accelerate drug discovery and development, and enhance access to healthcare. The overall impact that AI will have on the well-being of individuals who provide and receive care, however, is less obvious. This article examines the potential and pitfalls of AI in medicine through the lens of mattering and its importance to human flourishing. Mattering is a psychological construct that encompasses the human needs to be noticed, feel significant, and contribute. It arises from interpersonal interactions and is based on perceptions of our value within our communities and society. Mattering is inherently relational, is a significant contributor to psychological well-being, and may be at risk in the age of AI. The authors describe the foundations of mattering and its relevance to medicine; the potential impacts of AI on mattering in medicine from the clinician, patient, and trainee perspectives; and propose a framework for integrating AI into healthcare such that mattering is preserved for all stakeholders.

documents.abstract: In advancing Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for quality education, faculty members play pivotal role. Their health, especially mental health, is crucial for ensuring congenial learning environments. The current review explored the suitability of lightweight deep learning models for detecting burnout and assessing heart rate variability (HRV) using photoplethysmography (PPG) and remote photoplethysmography (rPPG). As the traditional stress assessment methods are time-consuming, physiological monitoring by artificial intelligence coupled with these signals offers an alternative scalable and non-invasive method. The findings are summarized in three key areas: technical advancements in lightweight deep learning architectures for physiological signal processing; academic research on faculty burnout in the Indian context; and existing mental health policies of regulatory bodies such as the UGC, AICTE, BCI, and PCI. The results indicate that these models can achieve high accuracy in detecting stress using PPG or rPPG in controlled settings. Further, the results indicated the need for targeted AI-driven mental health and wellness policies to support faculty well-being within the accepted legal frameworks.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Introduction Traditional ethnic sports such as Zhuang Daoyin demand precise movement, yet conventional demonstration–imitation–verbal correction limits feedback timeliness and individualization. Artificial intelligence (AI) real-time posture feedback offers a scalable option, but most evaluations emphasize technical outcomes and overlook learning processes. Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study tested whether and how AI real-time feedback improves motivation and motor skill by engaging basic psychological needs, with competence as the hypothesized pathway. Methods In a 12-week field experiment, 12 intact classes (307 students; control n = 152, AI n = 155) were randomly allocated at the class level to an AI real-time feedback group or a traditional teaching group; three instructors each taught two classes per condition. Both groups received identical instruction; conditions differed only in feedback source during practice (RTMPose-based concurrent vs. teacher-led terminal feedback). Need satisfaction, motivational regulation (relative autonomy index, RAI), motor skill, and course satisfaction were assessed at pre- and post-test, and analyzed with linear mixed models and structural equation modeling (lavaan, MLR). Results The AI group showed significantly greater gains in competence ( d = 0.36, p = 0.003), autonomy ( d = 0.40, p = 0.001), motor skill ( d = 0.30, p = 0.010), and learning interest ( d = 0.38, p = 0.003), whereas relatedness was unaffected ( p = 0.974); intraclass correlations were negligible. In the structural model (CFI = 0.94, RMSEA = 0.04, SRMR = 0.04), group predicted competence ( β = 0.17), competence predicted RAI ( β = 0.34), and RAI predicted motor skill ( β = 0.30); the autonomy and relatedness paths were nonsignificant. The effect of AI feedback on motor skill was fully mediated by the competence-to-RAI sequence (indirect p = 0.023; direct p = 0.097). Discussion AI real-time feedback improved motor skill by strengthening competence and supporting motivational internalization, while leaving relatedness unaffected—providing discriminant evidence that the tool acts through its affordances rather than diffuse enthusiasm. Systems enhancing performance and learning should prioritize feedback that makes progress legible, within a human–AI division of labor where teachers provide relational support. In conclusion, AI real-time posture feedback can enhance motivation and motor skill learning by satisfying learners’ competence need.

Activation steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide large language model (LLM) responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly nonsteerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided framework for activation steering that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: 1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; 2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and 3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

Emerging technologies are increasingly used to support intercultural learning, yet evidence on the distinct effects of artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR) remains limited. This systematic review and three-level meta-analysis synthesized 17 studies published from 2020 to July 2026 (77 effect sizes) to examine cognitive, attitudinal, and behavioral outcomes. The overall effect was large and significant (Hedges’ g = 0.965, 95% CI [0.580, 1.350], p < .001), although heterogeneity was substantial. AI-supported interventions also showed a significant positive pooled effect (g = 1.150, 95% CI [0.744, 1.555], p < .001). AR showed a significantly larger estimated effect than VR (β = −1.481 for VR relative to AR, p = .017), but this difference was not robust to excluding one AR study. Academic level (F (1, 75) = 17.27, p < .001) and sample size (F (2, 74) = 3.873, p = .026) were significant moderators, with larger effects in K–12 and larger-sample studies. However, these exploratory comparisons involved uneven technology distributions and only two K–12 studies. Outcome domain did not significantly moderate effects. Sensitivity analyses supported the stability of the overall pooled effect. The findings indicate that emerging technologies can improve intercultural learning, while better-balanced comparative studies are needed to identify which technological approaches are most effective.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI and large language models is reshaping how work is organised and how employees engage with emerging technologies. Yet the role of culture in these responses remains poorly understood and is often inferred from contextual proxies rather than measured directly. This systematic review synthesises empirical journal studies of explicitly AI-framed technologies in workplace and professional settings, with particular attention to directly measured cultural values and culturally situated conditions. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO via EBSCOhost and PubMed identified 910 records. A complete re-screening during revision of an updated title-distinct set of 691 records yielded 13 eligible studies. The evidence base was small, heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Only four studies directly examined named cultural-value constructs, while the remainder represented culture through national context, organisational culture, professional culture or locally grounded frameworks. Across studies, employee responses ranged from acceptance, trust and optimism to uncertainty, perceived threat, autonomy, professional identity, human–AI collaboration, innovation, job crafting and adaptation. Rather than indicating a consistent cultural effect, the findings suggest that cultural influences are contingent on how culture is operationalised and on the organisational and professional settings in which AI is introduced. Stronger multilevel designs, more direct measurement of cultural values and clearer separation of cultural, national and organisational influences are needed before robust cross-cultural conclusions can be drawn.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, it presents new opportunities to enhance the accessibility of instructional materials. This session examines how Microsoft Copilot, Adobe AI, and built-in Windows 11 features such as live auto-captions can support more accessible content creation and remediation across Microsoft 365 applications and PDF workflows. Focusing on commonly used instructional formats including Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and PDFs shared through learning management systems, this presentation highlights how AI tools can assist in identifying and addressing accessibility barriers. Examples will illustrate how Copilot can support content development, organization, and alternative text generation, while Adobe AI tools streamline improvements to PDF structure, tagging, and usability. Windows 11 auto-captioning features will also be discussed as a way to enhance access to audio and video content. The session explores practical approaches for integrating AI-supported accessibility strategies into existing teaching and course design workflows. Attention is given to aligning these approaches with accessibility standards and inclusive teaching practices while maintaining efficiency for instructors, instructional designers, technologists, and teaching assistants. Attendees will gain insight into key strategies, considerations, and potential applications of AI to create more inclusive, accessible instructional materials.

Agentic AI extends Generative AI from response generation to goal-oriented digital execution. Enterprise agents can interpret objectives, plan tasks, retrieve knowledge, invoke tools, call APIs, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and adapt execution based on intermediate results. These capabilities require a reference architecture that separates probabilistic reasoning from deterministic enterprise controls. This paper proposes an Enterprise Agentic AI Reference Architecture spanning experience, agent orchestration, planning and reasoning, enterprise knowledge, memory, model runtime, tool and integration services, identity, policy enforcement, observability, security, Responsible AI, and human oversight. The architecture integrates SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Integration Suite, enterprise APIs, RAG, Knowledge Graphs, and cloud-native services. It provides patterns for secure and scalable agent deployment across hybrid and multi-cloud environments while preserving accountability, bounded autonomy, operational resilience, and business value.

Artificial Intelligence is becoming embedded in enterprise decisions, customer interactions, software engineering, operations, and autonomous workflows. As adoption expands, organizations must manage not only model performance but also trust, risk, security, compliance, explainability, privacy, resilience, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise AI Trust, Risk and Compliance (AI TRiSM) Framework that integrates enterprise architecture, AI governance, model risk management, cybersecurity, privacy, Responsible AI, legal compliance, observability, and lifecycle controls. The framework establishes governance domains for AI inventory, risk classification, model assurance, data and prompt governance, identity, security, human oversight, monitoring, incident response, regulatory evidence, and recertification. It supports predictive AI, Generative AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Agentic AI across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale AI while maintaining measurable trust, bounded risk, defensible compliance, and clear accountability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Autonomous enterprises increasingly combine Artificial Intelligence, Agentic AI, automation, event-driven platforms, digital twins, data products, and intelligent decision services to execute business processes with reduced manual intervention. Traditional enterprise architecture methods are often insufficient when systems can plan, reason, act, learn, and coordinate dynamically across organizational boundaries. This paper proposes an Enterprise Architecture for Autonomous Enterprises framework that aligns business capabilities, operating models, data, applications, integration, AI, security, governance, and human oversight. The framework introduces architectural principles for bounded autonomy, policy-driven execution, decision rights, digital workforce governance, real-time observability, resilience, and continuous assurance. It also defines reference layers, implementation stages, governance gates, and measurable outcomes. The proposed approach enables organizations to scale autonomous operations while maintaining accountability, interoperability, trust, regulatory readiness, and business control.

Modern enterprises are shifting from project-centric data pipelines toward reusable data products that are owned, governed, discoverable, and consumed through standardized interfaces. This transformation requires an architecture that connects business domains, semantic models, data contracts, quality, lineage, metadata, security, interoperability, observability, lifecycle governance, and measurable value. This paper proposes an Enterprise Data Product Architecture Framework that defines the structural and operating principles required to design and manage data products across SAP and non-SAP landscapes. The framework integrates SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP HANA Cloud, APIs, event-driven integration, metadata catalogs, data quality services, data sharing, analytics, and AI consumption. It establishes product roles, architecture layers, data contracts, governance controls, service levels, lifecycle stages, and KPIs/KRIs. The proposed approach enables organizations to reduce duplication, improve trust and reuse, accelerate analytics and Artificial Intelligence, and strengthen business accountability for enterprise data.

Enterprises are rapidly moving from isolated copilots toward ecosystems of specialized AI agents that collaborate across business processes, data domains, applications, and cloud platforms. Multi-agent systems can improve decomposition, parallel execution, specialization, resilience, and decision quality, but they also introduce architectural challenges involving identity, delegation, shared memory, tool access, message routing, conflict resolution, security, observability, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework that defines a layered architecture for agent discovery, orchestration, inter-agent communication, knowledge grounding, enterprise integration, policy enforcement, runtime isolation, and human oversight. The framework combines enterprise architecture principles, Zero Trust, Responsible AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graphs, API governance, event-driven integration, and lifecycle management. It enables organizations to design scalable multi-agent environments in which specialized agents can collaborate safely while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, data protection, and measurable business outcomes across hybrid and multi-cloud landscapes.

BackgroundCutting-edge deep learning algorithms are applied to epileptic seizures to uncover hidden patterns and achieve high accuracy. Post hoc algorithms explain black-box models but do not reveal the detailed workings of the algorithms. Therefore, intrinsic methods overcome these issues; however, they suffer from improper use of indicative metrics and performance-to-accuracy trade-offs.ObjectiveThis study implements a lightweight multimodal explainable Neural Network for real-time early warning of epileptic seizure onset.MethodsPeople with drug-resistant epilepsy across all age groups who had regular follow-up at Emanuel Mental Specialized Hospital in Ethiopia during the data collection period were the study population. EEG recordings were performed using the 10/20 system. A pretest was conducted two weeks before actual data collection. EDFbrowser was used for preparing the dataset in CSV format. Learned and identity self-explainable neural network algorithms were used to develop a model. In addition to classical evaluation metrics, explicitness, faithfulness, stability, and clear patterns behind predictions were used. Ethical approval was also obtained from the institutional review board (IRB) with reference number No: AM/146/2/36.ResultsLearned and identity self-explainable neural networks were developed and compared. The models' accuracies are 96.524% and 95.328%, and their stability mean values are 99.88% and 99.88%, respectively. Additionally, explicitness values of 0.0055 and 0.01197 were achieved, respectively.ConclusionThe results demonstrate that using a self-explainable neural network is a promising step toward responsible and transparent artificial intelligence. Comparing the two models shows that the learned self-explainable neural network is slightly more optimistic than the identity self-explainable neural network.

Chapter 8 introduces the concept of the vocation economy, extending the original framework of the author’s first book of this trilogy, On Vocation – How to Align Your Purpose with Your Profession , from the inner journey of individuals to the broader dynamics of organisations, markets and societal systems. It argues that vocation is no longer merely a personal search for meaning but an emerging organising principle for institutions operating in an age of technological acceleration, social disruption and growing demand for authenticity. As individuals seek alignment between their values and their work, organisations are increasingly challenged to embed purpose into their strategy, culture and governance. When personal vocation and organisational purpose diverge, disengagement, mistrust and institutional fragility follow. Drawing on the author’s professional experiences and insights from thinkers such as Viktor Frankl, Peter Drucker, Amartya Sen and Mariana Mazzucato, the chapter frames vocation as a systemic force shaping the future of work and economic life. It explores how talent, capital and innovation increasingly flow towards institutions that demonstrate coherence between purpose and practice. At the same time, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence amplify the ethical stakes of this transformation, making it essential that technological progress remains anchored in human dignity and accountability. Ultimately, the chapter positions the vocation economy as the next evolutionary stage of capitalism – one defined by alignment between individuals, organisations and societal needs – where purpose becomes the foundation of resilience, trust and long-term flourishing.

Abstract Background The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into higher education is rapidly accelerating, yet the educational ecosystem appears largely unprepared for the scale and speed of adoption. Our recent international survey of over 1,200 university students and postdoctoral fellows in the medical and life sciences found that while more than 80% had used GenAI tools, the vast majority had received no formal training, and many were unaware of any institutional policies governing their use. This gap between adoption and institutional preparedness may pose risks to research integrity if left unaddressed. Main body Existing research supports a coordinated, evidence-informed approach to AI education in research performing organizations (RPOs), grounded in principles of research integrity, equity, and critical engagement with technology. First, GenAI literacy must be embedded as a core competency in scientific and clinical education, equipping students to critically evaluate tool outputs, recognize hallucination and bias, and understand the distinction between AI-generated inaccuracy and deliberate research misconduct. Second, traditional frameworks for academic integrity would benefit from re-examination. Today, GenAI tools have fundamentally disrupted established notions of authorship, originality, and plagiarism, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance leaves students and educators navigating these questions without support. Third, RPOs must develop clear, transparent, and context-sensitive policies on GenAI use by embedding responsible AI education into curricula, equipping learners not only to use these tools effectively, but to question, verify, and critique their outputs in ways that uphold scientific standards. Conclusion RPOs have an urgent responsibility to move beyond reactive responses and toward proactive strategies that uphold scientific standards, promote equity of access, and prepare the next generation of researchers and clinicians to engage with GenAI responsibly and ethically.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter introduces the concept of personalised learning, learning analytics, automated assessment, and the emergence of generative AI in transforming education, while also highlighting the ethical, privacy, governance and cybersecurity dilemmas that arise with implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. The chapter gives an overview of ethical and responsible use of AI in education, starting with an examination of the educational AI ecosystem, followed by a discussion of data lifecycle in education, and concluding with an exploration of algorithmic bias, transparency, informed consent, data ownership, surveillance and risks posed by generative AI. It outlines the principles of responsible data governance, privacy-by-design, privacy-preserving methods and other international frameworks like GDPR AI Ethics and OECD Principles. The topics of AI-driven cybersecurity, key practice insights for both educators and institutions, developers and policymakers, and future research areas for AI are also discussed.

documents.abstract: Introduction Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and its sub-theory Cognitive Evaluation Theory (CET), the present study examines how ethical leadership relates to employees’ job crafting through intrinsic motivation, and how this indirect relationship is contingent on job feedback. We proposed that ethical leadership is positively related to job crafting via intrinsic motivation, and that job feedback moderates this indirect effect by providing competence-relevant informational cues. Methods We tested our hypotheses using two-wave data collected from 102 employees in the customer service department of a gaming company in northern China. Results The results provided preliminary evidence of a moderated mediation pattern, suggesting that the indirect association between ethical leadership and job crafting through intrinsic motivation varied as a function of job feedback. Discussion These findings extend research on ethical leadership and job crafting by clarifying intrinsic motivation as the motivational mechanism and job feedback as a key boundary condition. The theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education requires frameworks that promote its responsible, flexible, transparent, and academically rigorous use. This paper first provides a literature review of the current state of the art on the ethical use of GenAI in higher education between 2023 and 2025. The aim is to examine how higher education institutions, researchers, and educators have responded to the ethical challenges associated with integrating GenAI into teaching and learning. It then presents a descriptive and analytical study of the Russell Group's principles for the use of GenAI in higher education (2023)—transparency, equity, reliability, accountability, and autonomy—and analyses the information published on the websites of its twenty-four member universities. This analysis makes it possible to determine the extent to which similar regulatory principles have been adopted by other institutions and to evaluate the benefits of establishing clear policies and procedures to support a transparent and effective academic framework.

documents.abstract: This paper examines the ethical and philosophical implications of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology—not for human society, but for “non-human beings” and the Earth’s ecosystems.Conventional discussions of AI ethics and the philosophy of technology have consistently remained within an “anthropocentric” framework focused on human labor, copyright, or whether AI possesses a mind equivalent to that of humans.However, modern AI is already deeply penetrating the natural world.In this paper, from the perspectives of environmental philosophy and bioethics, we present three core paradigms: I) the redefinition of the dignity of life brought about by the translation of animal language using AI; II) signal pollution in the natural world caused by digital technology (ecological deepfakes); and III) the environmental burden and infringement on the right to life of other organisms resulting from the materiality of computation.In conclusion, we argue that future AI ethics must undergo a paradigm shift toward “Environmental AI Ethics,” which encompasses all life systems beyond humans. documents.abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness, pedagogical quality, and user experience of ChatGPT and two AI-powered educational tools, Magicschool.ai and Eduaide.ai, in generating lesson plans for teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL). The analysis examined the extent to which the generated lesson plans align with modern pedagogical principles, demonstrate usability, clarity and adaptability, and address key EFL instructional needs, including grammar accuracy, vocabulary development, student engagement, and classroom practicality. For each tool, two different prompts were used to produce distinct lesson plans, which were subsequently evaluated by the researcher in terms of quality and instructional efficiency. The comparative analysis indicates that all three AI-platforms demonstrate pedagogical coherence, alignment with EFL approaches and methods. In terms of creativity, flexibility, accuracy, they do not seem to present great differences. However, they differ in their degree of practicality, differentiation, and learner's active thinking.

Structural dam safety control is fundamentally based on visual inspections and on the analysis of monitoring data and their comparison with the expected behavior for a given load combination, which in turn is calculated with a predictive model. In recent decades, the development of machine learning algorithms has led engineers and researchers worldwide to explore their capabilities for predicting dam behavior and supporting safety assessment. Regardless of the model used, a prediction is generally obtained together with an expected model error, which is compared with the observed value in order to support decision-making. This process, however, requires the intervention of experts in dam engineering, and particularly in the prior behavior of the structure under analysis. In recent years, the emergence of generative artificial intelligence models has opened up considerable opportunities to improve processes in various fields, including civil engineering. The reported capabilities of these models make them well suited to some tasks in the field of dam safety, particularly for developing predictive models and interpreting their results. In this work, we tested ChatGPT to assess its potential in these tasks, using the data from the ICOLD 2022 Benchmark Workshop, in which 18 teams provided their best predictions of the behavior of an arch dam. ChatGPT was provided with the same problem description and monitoring data available to the participants and was asked, through brief and neutral prompts, to propose a modeling strategy, generate predictions for six response variables for short- and long-term periods, create the corresponding source code, and interpret the results from a dam safety perspective. The complete procedure was performed twice using the same information and prompts. The results show considerable potential for increasing productivity in building and applying machine learning models, with predictive accuracy comparable to that obtained by the Benchmark participants. ChatGPT achieved a lower mean absolute error than the participants’ average in 10 (first run) and 12 (second run) of the 12 variable–period combinations, and outperformed the best participant in one case. However, the interpretation of the results was considerably weaker, with important aspects being only partially addressed or overlooked. These findings highlight the potential of ChatGPT to assist in the development of data-based predictive models, but also reveal its limitations in terms of the domain-specific knowledge required to draw conclusions on dam safety.

Abstract Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.

Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients and clinicians to obtain medical information, yet their performance may change over time as models are updated. Male infertility is a guideline-sensitive field in which inaccurate or incomplete information may affect diagnostic evaluation, counseling, and treatment expectations. This study evaluated the year-on-year evolution of ChatGPT, Perplexity, and DeepSeek in responding to guideline-derived male infertility questions between 2025 and 2026. Results A total of 528 chatbot responses were evaluated from 88 European Association of Urology (EAU) guideline-derived male infertility questions answered by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and DeepSeek in 2025 and 2026. In 2025, significant inter-model differences were observed across all four scored domains, with Perplexity achieving the highest content-quality and expert-rated scores and DeepSeek showing the weakest performance. In 2026, DISCERN scores converged across models, whereas significant differences persisted for readability, Global Quality Score, and expert opinion. ChatGPT showed significant improvement across all four scored domains and achieved the highest Global Quality Score in 2026. DeepSeek demonstrated the most pronounced improvement, particularly in DISCERN and expert opinion scores. Perplexity improved in readability but did not show a parallel positive change in Global Quality Score or expert-rated clinical usefulness. Potential patient-safety concerns were identified in seven of the 88 DeepSeek responses from 2025, whereas no such concern was identified in the 2026 responses. None of the 528 responses contained an explicit recommendation considered likely to cause immediate or serious patient harm. Conclusions Performance changed in a model-specific rather than uniformly progressive manner. The findings represent sampled first-pass responses to clearly formulated guideline-derived questions rather than stable estimates of model performance or reproducibility. LLMs may support access to male infertility information, but verification against authoritative sources and appropriate human oversight remain necessary.

documents.abstract: Abstract Understanding how global change reshapes species distributions remains a central challenge in ecology, yet most global assessments treat environmental drivers as static, uniform, or aggregate influences. This obscures where, why, and how specific drivers generate ecological risk or opportunity. Here, we apply explainable machine learning to assess how climate averages, variability, extremes, and land cover are projected to reshape future distributions of 1,992 terrestrial mammals. Using Shapley Additive Explanations with species distribution models, we quantify the directional contribution of 16 environmental drivers and track how these contributions change over space and time. We propose two ecological diagnostics, directional turnovers and favorability shifts, that reveal where drivers switch from favorable to unfavorable, or the reverse, and where their influence strengthens or weakens without sign reversal. While not designed to infer causation, our framework assesses whether projected spatial patterns align with ecological expectations. We show that climate extremes impose intense but spatially restricted impacts, temperature-related drivers dominate exposure patterns, particularly for specialist species, and the same driver can impose risk in one region while creating opportunity in another. By decomposing projected biodiversity change into driver-specific signatures, our framework advances biodiversity forecasting toward a more actionable understanding of ecological risk and opportunity.

Since its launch, ChatGPT has become a widely used tool by students for classroom exercises and home assignments. This study examines the role of ChatGPT as an automatic writing evaluation (AWE) tool in assisting Vietnamese high school students in self-correcting grammar and vocabulary errors in their descriptive writing assignments. The participants were five 18-year-old students at a private high school in Ho Chi Minh City. Before utilizing ChatGPT to revise original drafts, the participants were tasked with writing seven assignments based on Cambridge English Key (KET) exam picture prompts. Data collection included pre- and post-ChatGPT-usage writing assessments, screenshots of revisions, and some questionnaires exploring feedback engagement and reasoning behind acceptance or rejection of ChatGPT’s suggestions. Results showed improved writing, highlighting ChatGPT’s strengths in correcting grammar and enhancing vocabulary. Students engaged deeply with feedback, selectively accepting or rejecting suggestions based on their writing context and demonstrating enhanced self-assessment and learning independence. This autonomy is noteworthy and valuable in large classrooms where teacher feedback is limited. However, the participants expressed mixed levels of trust in the tool, especially when the suggestions seemed unclear or incompatible with their writing style, and often sought teacher validation. While ChatGPT promotes autonomous learning, it should complement, not replace, teacher feedback.

Prompt engineering (PE) involves creating, improving, and deploying prompts to improve large language model (LLM) performance. Despite its increasing importance, many students lack skills in this area. Although frameworks for prompt design and process exist, theory-based instructional tools for improving prompt engineering skills are uncommon for developing collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills in Robotics Education. This study adopted a PE strategy in AI-assisted robotics education, particularly for developing CPS. PE has four scaffolding stages: Alignment, Adaptation, Autonomy, and Innovation, and was analysed through four PE codes: Alignment Specification, Adaptive Refinement, Auditing, and Innovation. This study adopted a non-randomised, multi-site, criterion-group comparative design, with 243 undergraduate students categorised according to their ability group. This study used epistemic network analysis (ENA) to identify the co-occurrences of PE and CPS skills and examine the differences in conversation patterns among ability groups. The findings revealed distinct PE–CPS discourse configurations across ability groups. These results underscore the pedagogical value of scaffolding in developing PE skills and fostering students’ productivity in a synergetic learning environment.

Argumentation has been widely used as a discussion activity in the English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom. Nevertheless, peer argumentation combined with generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) remains limited despite increasing recognition of GenAI usage among EFL learners. To address this gap, we adopted the pragmatic-dialectic approach to argumentation and the proposition of intersubjectivity, and explored the argumentation process of six Chinese undergraduate students in their English newspaper reading course. A qualitative case study was used to analyze transcripts of peer argumentation, responses to an open-ended questionnaire and screenshots of chats with GenAI. Findings showed that students' peer argumentation was at a dynamic continuum, shifting from GenAI-dominated pseudo-argumentation with lowly dialogic moves to GenAI-coexisted authentic argumentation with highly dialogic moves. The study also yielded explanations for the changes, which involved the reciprocal awareness of human and/or GenAI, the outcome and the process of constructing a shared new understanding among heterogeneous interlocutors. The findings provided insights for the educational significance of the argumentative activities centered on the intersubjectivity in GenAI-coexisted language learning settings.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots have increasingly become part of many university students' English as a second language (L2) learning. However, little is known about how students in general foundation programmes use them during the move from Arabic-medium schooling to English-medium higher education. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study examined GenAI chatbot use among foundation-year students at a private university in Oman. A questionnaire (N = 262) covered usage patterns, perceived usefulness for L2 skills, AI output verification practices, challenges and support needs, and was followed by two focus groups (n = 15). Results showed that ChatGPT was the dominant tool (91.2%) that students accessed mainly by smartphone (80.5%). The most common frequency was "sometimes" (47.3%), while 42.4% of respondents reported using chatbots "always" or "often". Most students (57.6%) switched between English and Arabic while interacting with GenAI chatbots. Students rated chatbots as clearly useful for writing, speaking and reading, but not for listening. They also valued grammar and vocabulary corrections by chatbots more than their feedback on writing or speaking assignments. More than two-thirds of respondents preferred teacher feedback on their writing (72.9%). The most frequently reported challenges were incorrect information (43.5%) and unclear responses (35.1%), while the most common verification strategy of generated content was asking a teacher (46.2%). Focus-group participants described purpose-driven but largely unplanned prompting, translation-mediated comprehension, concern about overreliance, inconsistent teacher stances, and a need for classroom-embedded guidance. Chatbot use for L2 learning among foundation-year students can be interpreted as a tool-mediated activity largely outside formal L2 instructional design, with teachers as epistemic anchors. The study recommends early, skill-specific, teacher-mediated AI literacy instruction in foundation programmes.

This article examines the role of rural extension in scaling up agroecology in Brazil, arguing that such a transition depends on institutional mediations capable of linking knowledge, public policies, and territorial practices. By revisiting the principles of agroecological rural extension and analyzing their institutionalization within the National Policy for Technical Assistance and Rural Extension (PNATER), the study shows a progressive dilution of these principles throughout policy implementation. At the same time, it highlights the limited academic engagement with the interface between agroecology and rural extension. Based on this diagnosis, the article proposes a strategic agenda to strengthen agroecological rural extension, structured around four axes: progressive reframing of PNATER, valorization of sociotechnical arrangements, strengthening of training processes, and consolidation of a dedicated research agenda.

Background: Low back pain can restrict functioning through interacting symptoms, beliefs, and contextual demands. Qualitative inquiry can clarify how these influences are experienced. Objective: To explore perceived influences on disability and how they interact to restrict or support everyday functioning among adults with persistent low back pain. Methods: An interpretive qualitative study used purposive maximum-variation sampling to include 18 adults aged 25–66 years. Individual semi-structured interviews explored symptoms, movement, sleep, work, family roles, healthcare, and self-management. Oswestry Disability Index scores informed lower-, moderate-, and higher-disability sampling profiles. Interview material underwent reflexive thematic analysis, including examination of contrasting accounts and author review of interpretations. Results: Participants comprised 10 women and eight men; five had lower, seven moderate, and six higher disability profiles. Five themes were developed: Living with Unpredictable Pain; Fear, Threat, and Shrinking Activity; Caught Between Recovery and Livelihood; Support, Dependence, and Identity; and Clinical Explanations, Confidence, and Control. Accounts connected restrictions with anticipated flares, perceived damage, poor sleep, work and financial pressures, and changing family roles. Contrasting accounts described participation alongside pain when movement felt manageable and support preserved involvement. Conclusion: Disability was experienced within the interaction of symptoms, interpretations, relationships, and practical circumstances. Assessment and rehabilitation should consider barriers to meaningful participation alongside pain. Keywords: low back pain; disability; qualitative research; biopsychosocial factors; fear avoidance; self-efficacy; occupational health.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are becoming increasingly embedded in medical education, providing students with on-demand support for learning, clinical reasoning, and academic tasks. However, the psychological and technological factors that shape medical students’ acceptance of these tools remain insufficiently understood. This study examined acceptance among medical students with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to include AI literacy (AIL) and perceived security and privacy (PSP), and by examining their associations with perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), attitude toward using GenAI (ATG), and behavioral intention to use GenAI (BIG). A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among medical students at Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences (HUMS), Iran, between May and June 2026. Eligibility required prior academic use of a GenAI chatbot. Data were collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model was assessed for reliability and validity, while the structural model was evaluated using path coefficients (β), coefficients of determination ( R ²), and effect sizes ( f ²). Of the 292 students invited, 267 completed the survey, and 252 participants with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots were included in the final analysis (mean age, 22.64 ± 2.28 years; 147 [58.3%] female). The measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. AIL was positively associated with PEOU (β = 0.479, p < 0.001), while PSP was positively associated with PU (β = 0.157, p = 0.005). PEOU and PU were positively associated with ATG, and ATG showed the strongest association with BIG (β = 0.524, p < 0.001). The model explained 38.7% of the variance in BIG, with R ² values ranging from 0.229 to 0.387 across the endogenous constructs. The findings indicate that medical students’ acceptance of GenAI chatbots is associated with AIL and PSP alongside the core TAM constructs of PEOU and PU, with ATG showing the strongest association with BIG. Strengthening AIL and establishing clear privacy and security policies may support the informed and responsible integration of GenAI chatbots into medical education.

documents.abstract: Feature engineering remains central to predictive modeling in computational biology, governing how DNA, RNAand protein sequences are converted into numerical forms amenable to machine learning. The field hasprogressed from compact composition based descriptors such as amino acid composition (AAC) and dipeptidecomposition (DPC) to correlation based representations (pseudo amino acid composition, PseAAC, pseudoK-tuple nucleotide composition, PseKNC), evolutionary profiles (position specific scoring matrices, PSSM), and,more recently, to deep representation learning and biological foundation models. This narrative review focuseson biological sequence prediction, with particular emphasis on proteins and structure derived features. Webegin with Chou's five step framework for predictor construction, benchmark curation and redundancyreduction using CD-HIT and MMseqs2, and the specific challenges of multi label and hierarchical prediction. Wethen survey handcrafted descriptors, feature selection and dimensionality reduction, and the adaptation ofnatural language processing methods to biological sequences, including k-mer embeddings, convolutional andrecurrent architectures, and protein and genomic foundation models, including Transformer models such asESM-2 and DNABERT-2, the ESMFold structure predictor, and Hyena based genomic models. We distinguishthree common adaptation strategies: frozen embedding extraction, full fine tuning and parameter efficient finetuning (PEFT) - and discuss hybrid fusion of handcrafted and learned features, structure founded encodings(DSSP, Foldseek 3Di, ProstT5, SES-Adapter), and the role of explainable AI (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients).Throughout we emphasize homology evaluation, nested validation to avoid selection leakage, confidencebased use of predicted structures, and cautious interpretation of attribution. We close with practical guidelinesfor choosing a representation under different data and compute regimes and outline open challenges.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the use of information and learning resources in Islamic Religious Education, including Fiqh learning, while raising concerns regarding pedagogy, the authority and validity of religious knowledge, and students’ ability to evaluate AI-generated information. This study examines the use of AI in Islamic education and synthesizes its implications for Fiqh learning, focusing on pedagogy, the authority and validity of religious knowledge, and religious literacy and AI literacy. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 25 scholarly articles published between 2020 and 2026 and retrieved from Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Indonesian scholarly databases GARUDA/SINTA. Searches used combinations of keywords related to artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, Islamic education, Islamic religious education, and fiqh education. Articles were selected based on their relevance to Islamic education or Fiqh learning and to the analytical dimensions of the study. Data were analyzed through coding, thematic categorization, cross-source comparison, and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that AI is increasingly used to support personalized learning, information exploration, learning-material development, and instructional interaction. However, its use also intensifies the need for source verification, information validation, and teacher guidance. The synthesis further highlights the importance of integrating religious literacy and AI literacy to enable students to evaluate AI-generated information critically and responsibly. Based on these findings, the study proposes an AI-assisted but teacher-guided Fiqh learning framework that positions AI as a learning support tool, teachers as pedagogical and knowledge mediators, and students as active evaluators of information.

Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human–AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT, is increasingly used by university students for explanations, summaries, problem-solving, feedback, and academic support. This paper examines whether such assistance supports learning or may encourage dependence that affects long-term retention and independent thinking. Methods: The study uses secondary research and a descriptive synthesis of published experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. No primary data were collected and no new statistical meta-analysis was conducted. Results: The reviewed studies generally report positive effects on academic performance and engagement. Reported effect sizes include approximately g = 0.712 across 69 experimental studies, Hedges’ g = 0.577 across 37 studies, and an effect size of approximately 0.804 across 57 studies. However, one randomized controlled study reported 45-day retention of 57.5% for a ChatGPT-assisted group compared with 68.5% for a traditional-learning group. Conclusion: GenAI can be a useful learning assistant when students actively use it for explanation, feedback, comparison, and clarification. However, completing tasks efficiently should not be treated as proof of deep or lasting learning. Students should retain opportunities for independent recall, reasoning, analysis, and problem-solving.
